sections.title: Payroll and accounting should explain the same restaurant week
sections.body: A payroll correction changes labor cost. A tip input affects payroll records. Payroll entries then have to reconcile into the books and the cash plan. Ready Margin keeps those handoffs connected so the owner is not rebuilding the same week across a payroll company, a bookkeeper and a spreadsheet.

sections.title: Restaurant payroll problems often start before the payroll system
sections.body: A missed punch, changed shift, incomplete tip input or late manager correction can create a payroll problem even when the payroll software itself works correctly. We organize the operating inputs, unresolved questions and approvals before cutoff, then carry the final payroll information into the accounting process.

sections.title: The accounting record keeps the operating context
sections.body: Restaurant accounting needs more than a generic ledger. POS settlements, payroll, delivery payouts, supplier bills and cash timing can move on different schedules. Ready Margin keeps open questions visible through reconciliation and close instead of forcing the owner to rediscover them after the month ends.

sections.title: New York responsibilities are documented, not assumed
sections.body: Payroll-tax, wage-and-hour, tax-filing and legal responsibilities can vary by engagement and jurisdiction. Ready Margin documents which operational and finance tasks are included, who approves payroll, which filings are handled or coordinated, and when a qualified tax, employment or legal adviser remains responsible.

sections.title: One recurring finance rhythm instead of separate providers to chase
sections.body: The goal is not to replace every system. It is to create a dependable operating rhythm around the systems already in the restaurant so payroll, bookkeeping, close, reporting and financial questions move through one clear responsibility map.

sections.title: Stabilize the facts before choosing the fix
sections.body: A restaurant under pressure may have incomplete books, unknown payables, tax obligations, payroll questions and several explanations for the same cash problem. The first job is to build a dated, usable view of cash, commitments, recent performance and unresolved records.
items: Books, payroll and payables status assessment
Food, labor and vendor-cost pressure review
Location or daypart performance review where the data supports it
Recurring follow-up against the agreed plan

sections.title: Separate timing pressure from a structurally weak model
sections.body: A restaurant can run short of cash because receipts and payments are badly timed, because one-time obligations hit together or because the operation is consistently spending more than it earns. Those situations require different responses, so the turnaround review should distinguish them before management cuts indiscriminately.

sections.title: Turnaround work needs operating follow-through
sections.body: A cost decision only matters when someone owns the next step. A supplier issue needs a vendor conversation, a labor issue needs manager action and a reporting issue needs a stronger close process. Ready Margin keeps the financial finding attached to the operating owner and the next review date.

sections.title: No consultant can guarantee recovery
sections.body: Restaurant results depend on sales, lease terms, capital, market conditions, management execution and other factors outside any adviser’s control. Ready Margin can organize the evidence, priorities and follow-through but does not promise profitability, financing, insolvency outcomes or a particular recovery result.

sections.body: A spreadsheet cannot decide whether a portion, ingredient, prep method or menu item should change. Ready Margin provides the financial evidence and workflow; the restaurant’s operational leaders keep the culinary and service decisions.
